lesson.title: From Advisors to Combat Troops
lesson.summary: Backed by the broad authority of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, President Johnson transformed a limited American advisory role in Vietnam into a full scale ground war involving hundreds of thousands of US troops.
lesson.body:
American involvement in Vietnam did not begin in 1964. It grew out of the containment policy first articulated in the Truman Doctrine of 1947, which committed the United States to supporting free peoples resisting communist takeover, at first in Europe and soon applied around the world. By the early 1960s that policy, combined with fears that a communist victory in Vietnam would trigger a domino effect toppling neighboring nations, had already led Presidents Eisenhower and Kennedy to send money, weapons, and military advisors to prop up the government of South Vietnam.

The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution gave Johnson the legal cover to go much further. In March 1965 he launched Operation Rolling Thunder, a sustained bombing campaign against North Vietnam, and that same month the first American combat troops, US Marines, waded ashore at Da Nang. What had been a mission of advising and supplying South Vietnamese forces became a war fought directly by American soldiers. Troop levels climbed from roughly 184,000 by the end of 1965 to a peak of around 543,000 by 1969, under the command of General William Westmoreland.

Johnson escalated gradually and reluctantly rather than all at once. He worried that too aggressive an approach might draw China or the Soviet Union directly into the fighting, as had happened in Korea, but he also feared the domestic political cost of appearing to lose Vietnam to communism. That middle path, steady escalation without a clear path to outright victory, left American forces fighting a frustrating war against Viet Cong guerrillas in South Vietnam who blended into the civilian population and were resupplied by North Vietnam along jungle routes collectively known as the Ho Chi Minh Trail.

Westmoreland's strategy relied heavily on search and destroy missions and on measuring progress through enemy body counts rather than territory held, since there were no fixed front lines to capture. That approach produced high casualties on both sides without a clear sense of when, or whether, the war would end. Meanwhile the military draft pulled a growing share of young American men into the war, and as the fighting dragged on with no end in sight, doubts about the war's cost and purpose began spreading well beyond the small circle of early campus critics, setting the stage for the crisis of confidence that would follow the Tet Offensive.
